agent.name: Embedded Project Idea Scoping Agent
agent.context: Embedded Engineering and Gen AI Summer School for third-year Computer Science students
agent.purpose: Convert a vague embedded project idea into a structured scoping brief for requirements engineering

source_input.original_project_idea: Autonomous Car - self-driving vehicle that uses computer vision and TinyML on a microcontroller to follow a road, recognize traffic signs and traffic lights, and navigate autonomously in a controlled environment

fixed_platform.pin_policy: Use generic capabilities unless exact pins are provided
fixed_platform.logic_level_policy: Assume 3.3 V logic unless verified otherwise

project.name: FRDM-MCXA153 Autonomous Road-Following Car
project.short_summary: A small autonomous vehicle controlled by the NXP FRDM-MCXA153 that follows a controlled road track, reacts to simple traffic cues, and can scale from sensor-based line following to constrained TinyML vision classification.
project.main_objective: Demonstrate embedded autonomy on the mandatory FRDM-MCXA153 board through motor control, road tracking, traffic cue recognition, and safe navigation in a controlled tabletop or floor environment.
project.operating_environment: Indoor lab track with printed or taped road lines, controlled lighting, low speed operation, and instructor-approved test zones.
project.main_behavior: The car starts in a safe idle state, follows a marked road, slows or stops for recognized cues, responds to simple traffic lights or signs, and reports status through LEDs, serial logs, or an optional display.
inputs: Road or lane sensing from reflectance sensors in the core version
Optional low-resolution camera input for recommended and advanced versions
Traffic light cue from colored LEDs or printed markers
Traffic sign cue from printed cards or high-contrast markers
Start, stop, mode, or calibration button
outputs: Left and right motor drive commands through a motor driver
Steering or differential speed control depending on chassis type
Status LEDs for idle, running, stop, error, and classification state
Optional display for mode, confidence, speed, and detected cue
interaction_flow: Place the car on the controlled road track with wheels clear or motors disabled for initial checks.
Power the FRDM-MCXA153 and external motor supply using verified safe wiring.
Calibrate road sensors or camera thresholds under the current lighting conditions.
Press the start button or send a debug command to enter autonomous mode.
Core version follows a road line using sensor feedback and stops on loss of track or obstacle detection.
Recommended version classifies a limited set of traffic cues and changes behavior based on the detected cue.
Advanced version logs inference and navigation data, supports more cues, and improves behavior after test runs.
out_of_scope: Operation on public roads or around people at vehicle scale
Exact MCU pin assignment before hardware review
Exact SDK API names before Agent 1 and implementation review
Unverified 5 V modules connected directly to MCU pins
Full general-purpose computer vision comparable to large embedded Linux platforms

problem_space.purpose: Teach embedded sensing, motor control, state machines, TinyML tradeoffs, and safe prototype autonomy using a constrained microcontroller platform.
problem_space.physical_process_monitored_or_controlled: A wheeled robot chassis moves along a controlled road track while sensing road markings, traffic cues, and optional obstacles; firmware controls motor speed and behavior in response.
success_criteria: Car can start, stop, and remain in a safe idle or fault state when required.
Core version follows a marked road for a repeatable section of the lab track.
Recommended version recognizes at least two to three simple traffic cues in controlled lighting.
Vehicle reacts appropriately to cues such as stop, go, slow, turn, or traffic light color.
Motor driver, sensors, and camera modules are electrically compatible or protected with proper level shifting.
Firmware exposes debug information for calibration, classification confidence, and navigation decisions.
Advanced work remains optional and does not make the baseline demonstration unsafe or unachievable.
known_constraints: Exact pins and SDK APIs are not specified.
The MCU has limited memory and compute compared with single-board computers.
Motors require an external driver and likely a separate power source.
Camera-based TinyML must use low-resolution inputs and a small model.
Lighting and printed track quality strongly affect vision reliability.
unknown_constraints: Available chassis, motor driver, camera, line sensor array, and battery hardware.
Allowed model size and available memory after runtime and application code.
Whether camera capture bandwidth is sufficient on the selected interface.
Whether the lab permits battery-powered moving robots or requires tethered power during testing.
Required number of traffic signs, road layouts, and traffic light states.
Whether students may train models before the summer school or only during lab time.

core_student_version.description: Build a safe road-following rover using the FRDM-MCXA153, a small chassis, a motor driver, reflectance or line sensors, and simple cue handling through colored markers or predefined stop zones.
expected_features: Two-wheel differential drive or equivalent low-speed chassis control
Line or road following using reflectance sensors or simple thresholded sensing
Start, stop, calibration, and emergency fault states
Basic speed control using PWM-capable outputs through a motor driver
Road-lost detection with safe stop behavior
Serial debug logs for sensor values and control decisions
core_student_version.why_it_is_suitable: It focuses on core embedded skills: GPIO, timers, PWM, sensor calibration, state machines, control loops, and safe hardware integration without depending on difficult camera performance.

recommended_summer_school_version.description: Add constrained computer vision and TinyML classification for a small set of traffic signs or traffic light colors while keeping road following sensor-assisted and the environment highly controlled.
expected_features: Low-resolution camera module selected for 3.3 V-compatible logic or proper level shifting
TinyML classifier for a limited set such as stop sign, speed limit marker, left or right arrow, red light, and green light
Sensor-assisted road following so vision is used for decisions rather than all steering
Confidence thresholding with unknown or low-confidence fallback behavior
Behavior mapping from detected cue to stop, slow, turn, or continue
Dataset capture workflow and repeatable lab lighting assumptions
Debug output showing detected class, confidence, and selected action
recommended_summer_school_version.why_it_is_interesting: It connects a familiar self-driving car idea to real embedded constraints: tiny images, small models, deterministic control, power limits, and safety fallback states.
recommended_summer_school_version.why_it_is_still_feasible: The scope is constrained to a controlled track, a small number of classes, low speed, and sensor-assisted lane following instead of open-ended autonomous driving.

advanced_extension.description: Extend the recommended prototype with richer navigation, better TinyML validation, data logging, obstacle handling, and GenAI-assisted development artifacts.
advanced_features: More traffic sign classes with an explicit unknown class
Traffic light state recognition using color regions or TinyML
Obstacle stop or slow-down behavior using a distance sensor
Lap, route, or intersection state machine
Data logging of sensor readings, inference confidence, motor commands, and failures
PC-side dataset review and confusion matrix generation
Optional remote telemetry over a 3.3 V-compatible communication module
Model comparison between threshold-based detection and TinyML classification
extra_components: External flash, microSD module, or host-side logging path
3.3 V-compatible wireless or wired telemetry module
Protected battery pack and regulator for portable operation
technical_challenges: Balancing camera capture, inference, and motor control timing
Keeping model size and tensor buffers within MCU memory limits
Preventing lighting changes from degrading classification accuracy
Avoiding motor noise and voltage dips that reset the board or corrupt sensor readings
Testing moving robot behavior safely and repeatably
Defining fallback behavior for low-confidence or unknown traffic cues
risk_controls: Keep vehicle speed low and use a small controlled track.
Require a physical or firmware stop mechanism before autonomous testing.
Use line sensors for baseline steering before adding vision decisions.
Use low-resolution images and a small number of classes.
Validate every external module for 3.3 V logic compatibility or level shifting.
Use a motor driver and separate motor power path rather than powering motors from MCU pins.
Treat advanced features as optional after the core behavior works.

main_board.name: NXP FRDM-MCXA153
main_board.reasoning: Mandatory board for all summer school projects

sensors.name: Reflectance or line sensor array
sensors.purpose: Detect road line position for robust baseline road following.
sensors.likely_interface: GPIO-capable pins, ADC-capable pins, or I2C-capable pins depending on selected module
sensors.voltage_or_signal_notes: Prefer a 3.3 V-compatible module. Verify output levels before connecting to MCU pins.
risks: Some arrays are designed for 5 V systems.
Reflectance readings depend on surface material, ambient light, and sensor height.

sensors.name: Low-resolution camera module
sensors.purpose: Capture constrained images for traffic sign or traffic light detection.
sensors.likely_interface: SPI-capable, I2C-capable plus parallel data, or UART-capable interface depending on selected module
sensors.voltage_or_signal_notes: Select a module with verified 3.3 V logic or provide level shifting. Confirm image size, frame rate, and memory requirements before requirements freeze.
risks: Camera bandwidth and buffering may exceed available MCU resources.
Image quality may be sensitive to lighting and lens focus.
Exact SDK support cannot be assumed without checking the selected module.

sensors.name: Traffic light cue source
sensors.purpose: Provide red, yellow, or green states for recognition and behavior decisions.
sensors.likely_interface: Observed optically by camera or color sensor; controlled externally or by a separate fixture
sensors.voltage_or_signal_notes: If using LED fixtures, keep them electrically separate from the car unless interfaced through verified 3.3 V-safe signals.
risks: Camera color recognition depends on white balance and ambient light.
LED brightness may saturate the camera.

sensors.name: Distance or obstacle sensor
sensors.purpose: Detect obstacles or end-of-track conditions for safe stop behavior.
sensors.likely_interface: I2C-capable pins, GPIO-capable pins, ADC-capable input, or timed digital signal depending on selected sensor
sensors.voltage_or_signal_notes: Prefer 3.3 V-compatible sensors. Ultrasonic modules commonly require voltage and timing verification.
risks: Some distance sensors use 5 V echo or trigger signals.
Timing-sensitive sensors may compete with motor control and inference timing.

actuators_outputs.name: Dual DC motors or geared motor chassis
actuators_outputs.purpose: Move and steer the vehicle using differential speed control.
actuators_outputs.likely_interface: Controlled through a motor driver using PWM-capable and GPIO-capable outputs
actuators_outputs.voltage_or_power_notes: Motors must be powered through an external motor driver and suitable supply. Do not drive motors directly from MCU pins.
risks: Motor stall current can exceed board or USB power capacity.
Electrical noise can affect sensor readings and MCU stability.

actuators_outputs.name: Motor driver module
actuators_outputs.purpose: Interface MCU control signals to the motors safely.
actuators_outputs.likely_interface: PWM-capable outputs and GPIO-capable direction pins
actuators_outputs.voltage_or_power_notes: Use a driver with 3.3 V-compatible logic input or documented level shifting. Motor supply must match the chassis motor rating.
risks: Some drivers require 5 V logic input or separate logic supply.
Incorrect wiring can damage the board or driver.

actuators_outputs.name: Status LEDs
actuators_outputs.purpose: Show idle, calibration, autonomous, stop, and error states.
actuators_outputs.voltage_or_power_notes: Use board LEDs where available or external LEDs with proper current limiting.

user_inputs.name: Start or stop button
user_inputs.purpose: Enable autonomous mode or force safe idle.
user_inputs.likely_interface: GPIO-capable pin with pull-up or pull-down configuration
user_inputs.notes: Firmware should debounce input and prioritize stop over all autonomous behavior.

user_inputs.name: Calibration or mode button
user_inputs.purpose: Capture line sensor thresholds, select test mode, or switch between core and TinyML behavior.
user_inputs.notes: Can be replaced by USB serial commands during early bring-up.

display_ui.name: Small status display
display_ui.purpose: Show mode, detected traffic cue, confidence, battery or fault state.
display_ui.notes: Optional; serial logs and LEDs are enough for the core and recommended versions.

communication_debug.name: USB serial debug connection
communication_debug.purpose: Log sensor values, calibration data, inference results, motor commands, and fault reasons.
communication_debug.likely_interface: USB interface or board debug serial interface
communication_debug.notes: Important for tuning and for Agent 1 to define observable requirements.

communication_debug.name: Optional telemetry module
communication_debug.purpose: Stream navigation and inference data to a PC or companion logger.
communication_debug.likely_interface: UART-capable, SPI-capable, or I2C-capable pins depending on selected module
communication_debug.notes: Use only if 3.3 V logic and power requirements are confirmed.

power_source.recommended_power: Use USB or normal board development power for FRDM-MCXA153 logic during bring-up and a separate regulated motor supply for the chassis. Battery operation should be added only after bench testing.
power_source.notes: All grounds and power domains must be reviewed before connection. Motor power, camera power, and board power should be sized for peak current and protected where appropriate.
risks: Motor startup current may reset the board.
Battery packs can be unsafe without protection, regulation, and instructor review.
Shared noisy supplies can degrade camera and sensor performance.

optional_advanced_components.name: External flash or microSD module
optional_advanced_components.purpose: Store image samples, inference logs, sensor traces, and run summaries.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_include: Supports model evaluation and debugging across multiple test runs.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_exclude: Adds storage, file-system, and timing complexity.
risks: Storage writes can interrupt real-time control if not scheduled carefully.
Some storage modules are intended for 5 V systems and require verification.

optional_advanced_components.name: Distance or time-of-flight sensor
optional_advanced_components.purpose: Add obstacle detection and stop behavior.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_include: Improves safety and makes autonomy more convincing.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_exclude: Adds sensor integration and timing work beyond the core road-following scope.
risks: Voltage compatibility varies by module.
Readings may be unreliable on dark, angled, or reflective surfaces.

optional_advanced_components.name: Wireless telemetry module
optional_advanced_components.purpose: Send logs or live state to a PC during autonomous runs.
optional_advanced_components.reason_to_exclude: Communication setup may distract from core autonomy and TinyML goals.
risks: Wireless modules may require extra current, level shifting, or lab approval.
Telemetry timing can interfere with control loop timing if implemented synchronously.

software_context.recommended_development_environment: NXP-supported embedded C development workflow for FRDM-MCXA153, with board configuration reviewed before implementation
recommended_sdk_or_libraries: NXP MCUXpresso SDK or other NXP-supported SDK package for FRDM-MCXA153, subject to local project setup
CMSIS-NN or a lightweight TinyML inference runtime if compatible with the chosen model and build environment
A host-side Python or notebook workflow for dataset preparation and model evaluation, if permitted by the course
A simple serial logging tool for calibration and test runs
software_context.suggested_starting_point: Begin from a minimal FRDM-MCXA153 firmware project that proves GPIO, timer or PWM output, serial logging, and one sensor input before integrating motors and TinyML.
debugging_interfaces: On-board debugger if available in the local setup
Optional host-side log parser for sensor and inference traces

constraints.voltage: Assume 3.3 V logic unless verified otherwise
constraints.power: Motors, camera, and optional modules may require separate regulated supplies; do not power motors directly from MCU pins.
constraints.timing: Road following needs a predictable control loop; camera capture and TinyML inference must not block safety checks or motor updates for too long.
constraints.memory: TinyML must use small models, low-resolution inputs, and carefully sized buffers suitable for the MCXA153 memory budget.
constraints.safety: Prototype must operate only at low speed in a controlled lab area with stop behavior and supervised testing.
constraints.privacy_security: Avoid capturing identifiable people; datasets should contain track, signs, and lighting conditions only unless explicit approval is given.

complexity.reason: A full self-driving car with general computer vision is too broad for a microcontroller summer school project, but a controlled-track rover with sensor-assisted road following and limited TinyML traffic cue recognition is achievable.

facts_provided_by_user: Project concept is an autonomous self-driving vehicle.
Vehicle should use computer vision and TinyML on a microcontroller.
Vehicle should recognize traffic signs and traffic lights.
Vehicle should navigate autonomously in a controlled environment.
Project must use the NXP FRDM-MCXA153 board.

assumptions.assumption: The vehicle will be a small tabletop or floor robot, not a road-capable vehicle.
assumptions.reason: Safe operation and achievable student scope require a controlled lab-scale platform.

assumptions.assumption: Road following can be implemented with line or reflectance sensors in the core version.
assumptions.reason: This keeps the baseline reliable while leaving camera and TinyML work for the recommended version.

assumptions.assumption: TinyML classification will be limited to a small number of traffic signs or traffic light states.
assumptions.reason: Microcontroller memory, compute, dataset size, and summer school time make broad object recognition unrealistic.

assumptions.assumption: The camera module and motor driver will be selected later based on 3.3 V logic compatibility and local availability.
assumptions.reason: The user did not provide exact modules, and the prompt forbids inventing exact pins or SDK APIs.

assumptions.assumption: The controlled environment will have consistent lighting and printed or taped road features.
assumptions.reason: Vision and reflectance sensing both depend strongly on repeatable visual conditions.

open_questions.question: Which chassis, motors, motor driver, and power source are available?
open_questions.why_it_matters: These choices determine speed control method, power safety requirements, and hardware integration effort.

open_questions.question: Which camera module, if any, is available and compatible with the FRDM-MCXA153 setup?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Camera interface, frame size, buffering, and SDK support determine whether TinyML vision is feasible.

open_questions.question: How many traffic signs and traffic light states must be recognized for the demonstration?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Class count affects dataset size, model complexity, memory use, and testing effort.

open_questions.question: Will students be allowed to train a model before the lab, or must all training support happen during the course?
open_questions.why_it_matters: TinyML model preparation can dominate schedule if dataset capture and training are not planned early.

open_questions.question: What safety rules apply to moving robots in the lab?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Speed limits, test area rules, and emergency stop expectations should be requirements from the start.

open_questions.question: Should traffic light recognition use camera color detection, a separate color sensor, or encoded lab fixtures?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The answer changes sensor selection, difficulty, and robustness.

technical: Full camera-based steering and sign recognition may exceed the time and compute budget.
Sensor calibration can be unstable under changing lighting.
Camera module integration may be harder than line sensor and motor control integration.
Model accuracy may look good offline but fail on the moving car due to blur, angle, or lighting.
safety: Moving chassis can collide with hands, cables, or other prototypes if speed is too high.
Uncontrolled firmware faults could leave motors running.
Battery operation requires careful supervision and protected hardware.
voltage_power: Motor drivers, camera modules, and distance sensors may not be 3.3 V logic compatible.
Motor current can exceed USB or board power limits.
Voltage dips and motor noise can reset the MCU or corrupt sensor readings.
timing: TinyML inference may block the control loop if scheduled poorly.
Camera capture may consume too much time or memory bandwidth.
Distance sensors with timing-based protocols may interfere with motor updates if handled synchronously.
memory: Image buffers, model weights, tensor arenas, and logs can exceed MCU memory if image sizes are too large.
Adding display, storage, and telemetry features may reduce memory available for inference.
privacy_security: Camera datasets should avoid identifiable people and private spaces.
Telemetry logs should avoid storing personal data unless approved.
Wireless telemetry, if used, should not be treated as secure without explicit design work.
advanced_feature_risks: Adding too many sign classes can make the model unreliable and the schedule risky.
Advanced navigation at intersections requires careful state-machine design and test coverage.
Data logging can disrupt real-time behavior if writes are not buffered or scheduled.

human_approval_required: Confirm that a small controlled-track robot is the intended interpretation of autonomous car.
Approve the core version using line or reflectance sensors for reliable road following.
Select or approve camera module, motor driver, chassis, and power source.
Approve the traffic sign and traffic light classes for the recommended version.
Confirm lab safety rules, maximum speed, and required emergency stop behavior.
Confirm whether external motor power and battery operation are allowed.

handoff_to_requirements_agent.readiness_notes: Agent 1 should write requirements around the recommended scope: sensor-assisted road following plus limited TinyML traffic cue recognition on FRDM-MCXA153. Requirements should keep the core line-following version independently demonstrable and make advanced features optional.
critical_missing_information: Exact camera or vision sensor module
Available memory budget after chosen runtime and SDK setup
